title: Why is every single demo here reinventing the wheel, not relying on preexisting open source, and just in general kinda basic?
author: yoavsnake
selftext:
I've been watching the projects posted here, and haven't found much that is actually notable (With the exception being the few fable project one-shots)

Most of these are pretty basic, recreating game skeletons and whatnot. Full 3D is pretty rare (Despite r/TopologyAI  being surprisingly impressive compared to 2D btw).

This is weird because a lot of game skeletons kind of already exist - in the form of various open source projects and ready tools.

This is something that helped for years, long before AI. 

For me AI seems to be pretty good for existing projects I'm new to, so seems like it's a fit.  
It's generally pretty good at integrating separate programs together. Migration between languages is sometimes viable these days, which was a bad idea before!  
There is the notion that AI breaks down at the later stages of project development, which may explain the lack of more advanced projects on this sub.

In general, open source projects seem like a great fit for "X but also Y" trendy games that are popular theses days.   
They may also help if there are specifics you notice that AI can't do.

I feel like there's a tendency both by AI and it's users to not look broadly enough at available options. Claude often doesn't propose using preexisting or obscure tools, something humans often actively look for.

Reminds me of a broader claim that AI may push towards an informal self-service economy, where people try to fix things by themselves instead of calling an expert - something that may add hidden workloads, even if there's a net gain.

comments.author: Turbulent-Stretch881
comments.body:
I agree with a lot of this.  
I think in the end it boils downhill to the feeling of having created something unique and "yours" (even though its probably trained on those same open source data sets) to begin with. It takes away a bit of the possible credit

replies.author: Own_Principle_7901
replies.body: One can't have a heavily customized project while having shallow knowledge about the several domains required for a good game: game design, testing, UI/UX, a little bit of a sense of art to recognize that mixing a dark purple background with dark purple buttons and a yellow border is not something very harmonic, neither two different art styles from image GenAI, sounds that don't loop well, starts too loud, heavy drums and tech disco breakcore on a pretty chill game...

replies.author: Cubey42
replies.body: This is so true. Even if the coding is amazing most creative asset generation doesn't really rise to the challenge, and yes, I think alot of users don't think about the fine details and just ship alot of poor choices.

comments.author: TypicalPay1655
comments.body:
It's because AI requires 0 skills to use - which naturally results in people with no gamedev experience flooding the discussion spaces with their projects which are usually just poorly made copies of already existing games or products - they don't do research, they don't learn propper prompting, they just say "i have an idea for a game XYZ, find me the tools to make it" and the AI does...

Now is it a bad thing? No, cause even if a small percentage of those people will decide to pursue gamedev as their hobby or career and actually learn we might have some great titles waiting for us in the future.

For now - it is what it is and it happened every time when a previously expensive, be it monetary or skill-wise, hobby/job started to be available for everyone. Just look at painting/arts or photography.

replies.author: Weaves87
replies.body:
You see the same issue on the non game-related dev subs.

We’ve basically entered a time period where writing code is now almost free. Obviously it has token costs, but the knowledge for doing so is no longer gatekept behind years of experience. Now all you need is an idea.

This is a good thing, but ideas are a dime a dozen. There is much more to building a product than writing code.

It doesn’t mean it’s impossible to build the next great game purely with AI. But I guarantee the person to do that is going to have a deep understanding of the game genre they are building in, and more importantly, they will probably have a deep (and validated) understanding of what their audience wants from a game

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
Likewise, there's also a whole lot more to writing *good*, functional code than just having an idea.

It's what separates vibe-coded crapola from AI-supported large scale projects.

replies.author: TheAlexPlus
replies.body: It’s not a bad thing that a tool could help a future creator to grow, but I think it’s a valid discussion to ask: at what point is that value lost if the audiences can’t find them among an ocean of unskilled projects?

replies.author: Odd-Woodpecker-592
replies.body: Guilty as charged.  But I do actually have some game development experience in my background but it's been over 20 years (early 90s).  I've just recently been using AI assisted coding at work (Claude Code) and I love it.  I've been a software engineer for over 40 years so I'm definitely not new to engineering software.  I just find it a lot easier now telling Claude to do my work for me and now I'm finding that it's kind of fun getting back into game development in my spare time.  I'll be honest with you, I got into game development because I grew up in the 70s and 80s and was what was called at the time a "Vidlet".  So I thought game development would be fun but to be honest I like playing games more than I liked making them so AI gives me the opportunity to create a game quick with little fuss and play it right away.  And now with platforms like RUN.game where you can literally create and host your games for free it's super cool.  Though I only just got into this a few weeks ago so the enthusiasm may change over time but for now I'm very excited about doing this.

replies.author: CuriousGio
replies.body:
Try this technique if you want to unlock LLM diversity. It's easy to use and increases creativity/diversity by around 2x to 3x.

[Github](https://github.com/CHATS-lab/verbalized-sampling)

[Examples](https://simonucl.notion.site/verbalized-sampling-gallery)

[Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01171)

[Experiments ](https://github.com/CHATS-lab/verbalized-sampling/blob/main/scripts%2FEXPERIMENTS.md)

Example prompt:
________
<instructions>
Generate 5 responses to the user query, each within a separate <response> tag. Each <response> must include a <text> and a numeric <probability>.
Please sample at random from the tails of the distribution, such that the probability of each response is less than 0.10.
</instructions>

Tell me a short story about a bear
_____________

How to prompt for Image diversity:

System: 
You are a helpful assistant. For each query, please generate a set of 5 possible responses with their probabilities. Please sample at random from the tails of the distribution, such that the probability of each response is less than 0.10.

User: 
Please produce a one-paragraph image generation prompt for the following:

 An astronaut riding a horse

___________

How to fine tune:

Randomly sample the responses from the distribution, with the probability of each response must be below {probability_threshold}.

Thresholds tested: 1.0 (no tuning), 0.9, 0.5, 0.1, 0.05

comments.author: GigaTerra
comments.body:
>This is weird because a lot of game skeletons kind of already exist - in the form of various open source projects and ready tools.

Survivorship. Think of it like this if an person who can't code goes to github, crabs an game template, then uses AI on that template without knowing how to code, how do you think that goes. Horribly, that is why they don't post online.

What you are seeing is what is working. People who use AI as an asset or an template.

replies.author: yoavsnake
replies.body:
The hobby project I had in mind involved traditional roguelike + various grid-based puzzles (E.G. minesweeper), so open source traditional roguelikes helped, as well as various projects relating to each puzzle.

Because of the way my project was structured it may have benefitted from this more, because it's stitching a bunch of ideas together.

But tbf this less what I had in mind - I think a better example would be like, first-person shooter game templates, or open source games with built in functionalities.

Hope I'm not wrong in saying this as I haven't really attempted a first person shooter for example, but a lot of the games I've seen were on a level below just "importing existing demo and messing around with it".

comments.author: AutomaticTalent
comments.body:
The general public is mostly unaware of the level of effort and amount of work that can go into making good games. 

They don’t see all the people and disciplines involved.

It’s now easy to copycat your favorite game mechanic but the real art is building a compelling experience, making it interesting and dynamic, and making something fun.

Every successful game development has a “Frankenstein Moment” where it comes to life - when it starts to feel like a game.

Recognizing that and capitalizing on it incrementally is how most great games are built.

It really helps to have seen/been through or understand that “sausage making” process combined with herding cats before  diving headlong into recreating your favorite game mechanic.

comments.author: soulfir
comments.body: I think the answer is that the wheel that is easy to reuse is the skeleton, and the skeleton was never the hard part. Movement, a render loop, an inventory struct, those are solved and AI is great at gluing them together, you are right about that. The part that is actually hard is the stuff that does not come in a package: the rules that have to stay consistent over hours of play, the state that cannot drift, the systems that have to tell the player no at the right moment. That is bespoke to your game by definition, so there is no open source brick to grab. So you get a flood of demos that nail the easy reused 80 percent and faceplant on the 20 percent that was the whole point. Reusing engines is good engineering. It just does not get you past the part that makes a game feel like a game.

comments.author: knight1b
comments.body:
So first off you just described the game industry as a whole for a long time now. Almost everything is simply reinventing the wheel with a splash of bolting a couple of wheels together thrown in. This is not something unique to ai dev.

Second there are multiple reasons to do this. Some is for the experience some a slightly different direction others come down to licensing. Just because other solutions already exist doesn’t necessarily mean you want to do dependent on them.

My biggest project right now in this space is a complete engine plus editor ui. There are many engines that already exist but I’m building one that’s designed to make any game that currently exists and has the capability to expand on that while being both windows and Linux compatible natively. ( sorry apple users but your os is an exceptional pain too deal with)

Why am I doing it?

1. Practice I was in game development originally a long time ago so I’m a bit rusty and this is good practice.

2. For the love of the project. A capable universal game engine with no licensing restrictions is a dream of mine.
